resident.chief_complaint: Squeezing feeling at the midsection and tingling sensations in both upper and lower extremities.
resident.history: The patient is a 49-year-old male. Symptoms started approximately three months prior to the initial visit with a squeezing feeling at the midsection and tingling sensations in both upper and lower extremities. He reported no difficulty in walking. He demonstrated Lhermitte's sign when extending the neck abruptly. He denied any sensory and motor change. A diagnosis of ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) of the cervical spine had been made before hospital admission.
resident.physical_exam: The patient denied any sensory and motor change on physical examination. Lhermitte's sign was elicited on abrupt neck extension. Motor power and reflexes are not documented.
key_positive_signs: Lhermitte's sign on abrupt neck extension
resident.past_history: Diagnosis of ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) of the cervical spine was made before hospital admission. No other past medical history is documented.
resident.public_message: This 49-year-old male presented with a squeezing feeling at the midsection and tingling in both upper and lower extremities, symptoms beginning about three months before presentation. He had no difficulty walking. The patient denied any sensory and motor change on physical examination; however, Lhermitte's sign was elicited on abrupt neck extension. Imaging showed OPLL from C2 to C5 with atlas hypoplasia, spinal canal stenosis from C1 to C5 with cord compression at the atlas ring and an intramedullary high signal intensity area. Preoperative JOA score was 15 points.

imaging.public_message: I have not seen the films and am reporting only the case record's imaging description: OPLL was described from C2 through C5, with spinal canal stenosis from C1 through C5 and especially marked canal narrowing with cord compression at the atlas ring. An intramedullary high-signal area was reported. The record does not specify compression direction or a graded stenosis severity. These findings correlate well with the reported Lhermitte sign and bilateral sensory symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord, most likely at C1-2 (atlas ring) given the marked canal stenosis and cord compression. Lhermitte sign and bilateral upper and lower extremity tingling with truncal squeezing are consistent with cervical myelopathy involving the dorsal columns and possibly spinothalamic tracts. Motor and reflex findings are not documented, so precise long-tract involvement is inferred.

red_flags.finding: Motor power and reflexes are not documented; sensory examination reportedly normal despite subjective tingling.
red_flags.rationale: This is an examination gap, not evidence of an alternative cause. Lhermitte sign is a positive finding and imaging shows cord compression, so the absence of documented motor/reflex changes does not undermine the myelopathic localization.

red_flags.finding: Marked canal narrowing and cord compression at the atlas ring due to atlas hypoplasia, distinct from the OPLL at C2-C5.
red_flags.rationale: If surgical decompression is planned primarily for OPLL at C2-C5, the upper cervical compression at C1-2 may require additional or different surgical consideration. The cord compression at the atlas ring is part of the same cervical myelopathy but could change the operative approach.

neurology.public_message: Findings localize to the cervical spinal cord, most likely C1-2, with Lhermitte sign and bilateral sensory symptoms. Imaging shows cord compression at the atlas ring and intramedullary signal change, correlating well (high match). Red flags: (1) Motor power and reflexes are not documented—a coexisting limitation, not an alternative cause; (2) Atlas ring compression from hypoplasia may change the surgical plan if decompression targets only OPLL levels. No symptom-imaging mismatch.

physiatrist_opening.proposed_duration: 3-6 months of structured conservative management with close neurological monitoring
preconditions_for_failure: Development of new objective motor weakness (MRC grade ≤4/5) or gait instability
Worsening of JOA score by ≥2 points from baseline of 15
Appearance of bladder or bowel dysfunction
Progression of intramedullary T2 hyperintensity or new cord compression on follow-up MRI
Persistent or worsening symptoms despite 6 months of conservative treatment
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge the imaging demonstrates significant stenosis and cord signal change; however, the patient currently presents with mild symptoms (JOA 15, no motor or gait deficits documented, only subjective tingling and Lhermitte sign). A structured 3-6 month trial of conservative management—cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, avoidance of high-risk maneuvers, and close neurological surveillance—is a reasonable first step. Surgical decompression is indicated only if there is objective neurological deterioration (new motor weakness, gait decline, sphincter involvement) or worsening T2 signal on follow-up MRI. The success rate of observation and conservative therapy in mild myelopathy without obvious motor deficit is approximately 40%, and a trial can be undertaken safely with frequent reassessment.

preconditions_for_failure: Development of new objective motor weakness (MRC grade ≤4/5) or gait instability
Worsening of JOA score by ≥2 points from baseline of 15

physiatrist_final.public_message: The Director and Deputy Director have reiterated the cord signal change and Lhermitte sign as reasons to favor surgery. These are the same findings I considered: intramedullary T2 hyperintensity without clinical myelopathy (JOA 15, no motor or gait deficits) does not mandate immediate decompression, and Lhermitte sign is a nonspecific indicator of cord irritation. The surgeons themselves acknowledge that a complete neurological exam is needed and that if objective myelopathy is not demonstrated, a short observation could be discussed. This aligns with my proposal: initiate a structured conservative program now, monitor closely, and intervene only if the predefined failure criteria are met or the pending workup reveals instability or progressive cord compression. No new finding has been presented that outweighs the risk of unnecessary surgery in a patient with mild symptoms.

vice_opinions.assessment: The patient has cervical myelopathy (JOA 15) from two compressive pathologies: congenital atlas hypoplasia causing C1 ring stenosis and OPLL from C2 to C5. The reported T2 cord signal and Lhermitte sign are objective evidence of cord dysfunction despite mild symptoms, and high cervical stenosis carries a risk of stepwise deterioration. Surgical decompression is indicated in my view, but the operative plan depends on missing data: complete motor/reflex examination, CT to characterize OPLL and atlas dimensions, and dynamic films to assess stability.
proposed_options: Posterior decompression from C1 to C5: C1 posterior arch resection for atlas stenosis plus C2-C5 laminoplasty or laminectomy, with instrumented fusion if instability or kyphosis risk is demonstrated.

Anterior decompression of the OPLL (e.g., C2-C5 corpectomy/ACDF) if the anterior mass is the dominant compression and C1 ring stenosis is judged non-contributory; this does not address atlas hypoplasia and is technically demanding at C1-2.
Structured conservative management with serial neurologic exams and MRI, as proposed by physiatry, with surgery reserved for objective deterioration.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior decompression from C1 to C5: C1 posterior arch resection plus C2-C5 laminoplasty/laminectomy with fusion as indicated.
disagreement_points: Physiatry recommends a 3-6 month conservative trial; I disagree, because T2 cord signal with C1 ring compression carries a real risk of stepwise deterioration, and 'mild symptoms' may be understated because motor/reflex data are missing.

The relative contribution of OPLL versus atlas hypoplasia to cord compression is not defined; this determines whether posterior decompression alone is sufficient or whether an anterior procedure must be considered.
Dynamic radiographs and CT occupancy measurements are needed before choosing laminoplasty versus laminectomy/fusion; without them, the fusion decision is premature.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree with proceeding to surgery now rather than a conservative trial?
If surgery, do you endorse a posterior C1-C5 decompression as the index procedure, or should we obtain CT/dynamic imaging and revisit anterior versus posterior?
Should the patient be listed for surgery after the additional workup, or scheduled based on current MRI alone?
vice_opinions.public_message: I assess this as early myelopathy from tandem high cervical stenosis: atlas hypoplasia and OPLL. The cord signal change and Lhermitte sign are objective and make me reluctant to observe. I favor posterior decompression covering C1 through C5 to address both levels. I acknowledge that a conservative trial remains defensible, but I would want a complete neurologic exam and CT before accepting it.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 49-year-old male with cervical myelopathy due to tandem stenosis: atlas hypoplasia with C1 ring cord compression and OPLL from C2 to C5. The presence of Lhermitte's sign and intramedullary T2 hyperintensity are objective indicators of spinal cord dysfunction, making observation less attractive, but the documented clinical severity is mild (JOA 15, no motor or gait deficits recorded). The workup is incomplete: a full neurological examination (reflexes, Hoffmann, Babinski, motor scoring), CT with reconstructions to define the C1 ring and OPLL morphology, and dynamic flexion-extension radiographs are essential before finalizing the surgical plan. I agree with the director that surgery is likely indicated, but the exact procedure depends on atlantoaxial stability and OPLL severity.
proposed_options: Posterior C1-C5 decompression with instrumented fusion if atlantoaxial instability or severe OPLL is confirmed
C1 posterior arch resection with C2-C5 laminoplasty if no instability and OPLL is not severe

Conservative management with close neurological and MRI surveillance (defensible only if the completed exam shows no objective myelopathy signs beyond Lhermitte; not my preference given the cord signal change)
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior C1-C5 decompression; instrumented fusion if instability or severe OPLL, otherwise C1 laminectomy with C2-C5 laminoplasty
disagreement_points: The clinical severity does not yet include documented long-tract motor signs; a JOA of 15 may overstate function if all items were not tested. I would not finalize surgery until a full exam confirms objective myelopathy signs beyond Lhermitte. If the exam is completely normal, a brief observation period remains defensible, though I still lean toward surgery because of the cord T2 signal.

The need for fusion versus laminoplasty should be determined not only by dynamic radiographs but also by CT assessment of the C1 ring dimensions and OPLL extent/type. C1 laminectomy alone may alter atlantoaxial stability, and a standard laminoplasty may not adequately decompress the hypoplastic C1 ring.

Physiatry's conservative trial has a modest but real success rate in mild myelopathy. I agree with the director that surgery is favored here, but the equipoise should be openly acknowledged when counseling the patient.
